analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal land deal that gives a sacred tribal site in Arizona to a copper mining company.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2014, Congress attached a provision to a must-pass defense bill that directs the Forest Service to hand over about 2,422 acres of Tonto National Forest land known as Oak Flat to Resolution Copper Mining. The area is sacred to several Apache and other tribes and is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. The Save Oak Flat Act would simply repeal that provision, canceling the land exchange before it happens. It never received so much as a committee hearing.
analysis.who_benefits: Western Apache tribes and other Native nations for whom Oak Flat is a sacred ceremonial site, plus outdoor users of the Tonto National Forest and residents who depend on the region's groundwater, which the bill's findings say the mine would deplete and pollute.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals section 3003 of the 2015 defense authorization act, which requires the mandatory transfer of Oak Flat to Resolution Copper regardless of the outcome of tribal consultation or environmental review [S2, S3].
The bill's findings state that Resolution Copper plans to use block-cave mining that will physically collapse the surface of Oak Flat, destroying sacred areas and contaminating water supplies [S3].

The findings state the 2014 provision was attached without normal legislative process, was pulled from House consideration twice as a standalone bill, and that an amendment to remove it was never allowed a vote [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Resolution Copper Mining, a joint venture of major international mining companies, loses the congressionally guaranteed land swap it needs to build what it describes as one of the largest copper mines in the United States, along with the jobs and copper supply the project would create.
analysis.who_pays_short: Resolution Copper and its mining backers

drawbacks.text: Repealing the exchange cancels the deal entirely, including the various parcels of private land Resolution Copper would trade to the public in return [S2], which supporters of the mine note would add to public holdings and local economies.
Copper is a strategic material for electrical infrastructure, and blocking the mine forgoes a major domestic copper source; the bill offers no alternative plan for that supply [S2, S3].

The repeal is absolute: it reverses a law already on the books rather than strengthening the environmental review or tribal consultation that critics of the 2014 provision said was missing, leaving the mine's backers a standing argument that the process was rigged against them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the tribes and communities directly affected, the stakes are permanent: the bill's own findings concede the mine would collapse the surface of a sacred site forever and pollute groundwater [S3]. Against that is a real but conventional cost — a delayed or relocated copper mining project of the kind evaluated routinely through normal environmental review. The main design weakness is that the bill restores the status quo instead of fixing the process flaws it documents; the mine's backers would retain the right to pursue the land through ordinary channels.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never held a hearing or vote, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sanders introduced the bill on June 15, 2017, joined by four Democratic cosponsors; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day [S1, S5].
The action history contains only those two actions — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote [S5].
The underlying land exchange it sought to repeal remains law: section 3003 of the 2015 defense act still mandates the transfer of the Oak Flat parcel to Resolution Copper [S2, S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Resolution Copper is better off: the congressionally mandated land exchange stayed in place untouched, with no committee ever taking up the repeal.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Resolution Copper and the mining industry

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Save Oak Flat Act to repeal the Oak Flat land exchange provision.

for.name: Apache and other Southwestern tribes
for.role: Tribal nations for whom Oak Flat is sacred
for.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the land transfer and supported repeal efforts to protect the sacred site.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over public land transfers
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: John McCain and Jeff Flake
against.role: Arizona's Republican senators and champions of the Resolution Copper land exchange
against.what_they_did: Long supported the Oak Flat land swap, which McCain helped attach to the 2015 defense bill as Armed Services chairman, keeping the exchange politically protected from repeal efforts.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken on the bill; its sponsor and all five cosponsors were Democrats or an Independent, and the committee's Republican majority never acted on it.

industries.industry: Copper mining (Resolution Copper, a Rio Tinto/BHP joint venture)
industries.note: Repeal would cancel the congressionally mandated transfer of Oak Flat, blocking a mine whose block-cave method would collapse the surface of a tribal sacred site and, per the bill's findings, deplete and pollute regional groundwater [S2, S3]. The company's gain depends on a land giveaway that ordinary process — environmental review and tribal consultation — would not guarantee, which is why its interest runs against the tribes and residents affected.
